subtitle: Implementation schedule for the TIP's new Telnet protocol

tldr.problem: The TIP (Terminal Interface Processor) needed to implement the new Telnet protocol, but because TIP changes affect many other hosts, a public schedule was essential.
tldr.mechanism: BBN published a schedule with target dates for each phase: basic design, options design, implementation of core options, and final deployment.
tldr.outcome: The roadmap allowed the network community to plan around the TIP changes, ensuring coordinated deployment of the new Telnet protocol.

today: RFC 688 was a planning document for a 1975 implementation project on the ARPANET. The TIP and the Telnet protocol have both been superseded by modern systems and protocols.

sections.title: The TIP's New Telnet Implementation
sections.content:
RFC 688 is a schedule from BBN for implementing the new Telnet protocol in the TIP (Terminal Interface Processor). The TIP was a network access device that allowed terminal users to log into other hosts on the ARPANET.

The RFC explains that implementing the new Telnet protocol had become the top priority for the TIP development team. Because what the TIP did affected how many hosts could serve remote users, the team shared its implementation schedule publicly so the network community could coordinate.
sections.eli5: The TIP was a box that let people use terminals to reach computers on the network. The team shared their work plan publicly because so many people depended on it.

sections.title: The Four-Phase Schedule
sections.content: The implementation plan had four major milestones, each with a target completion date in 1975. First, by July 18, the team would finish the basic design with a version that could negotiate Telnet options but refused all of them. Next, by mid-September, the design of the options themselves would be complete. Third, by mid-November, a working version supporting the basic option set would run on the TIP: Binary Transmission, Echo, Suppress Go-Ahead, Timing Mark, and RCTE. Finally, by the end of 1975, the team would resolve any problems with host interactions and deploy a stable version of the TIP running the complete Telnet protocol.
sections.eli5: The schedule had four steps with dates from mid-1975 to year end. Each step added more features until the whole Telnet protocol worked on the TIP.

sections.title: Impact on the Network
sections.content: Because the TIP served many hosts and users, delays in its implementation could slow adoption of the new Telnet protocol across the network. By making this schedule public, BBN allowed other host administrators and system planners to anticipate when the TIP would support the new protocol and to schedule their own transitions accordingly. This kind of coordinated planning was essential for maintaining network interoperability during major protocol changes.
sections.eli5: Many computers on the network relied on the TIP, so its schedule mattered to everyone. Publishing the dates helped everyone else plan their own work.
